# Restorative Agrisolar Design {.unnumbered}

::: {.draft-note}
**Working draft, circulated for comment.** Some citations are
[not yet verified](chapters/sources.qmd) and are marked where they appear, and the
[evidence base](chapters/open-issues.qmd) says what is established, what is
inferred, and what nobody has measured.
:::

::: {.welcome}
Solar and farming want the same flat, open, well-drained ground. An array can carry pollinator habitat or gravel, slow runoff or redirect it, shade stock, retire irrigation demand, or help sustain a farm. Those are design decisions.

[**Agrisolar**](chapters/terminology.qmd#term-agrisolar) names solar generation on agricultural land, whether or not production continues below it. [**Agrivoltaics**](chapters/terminology.qmd#term-agrivoltaics) is the narrower case of crops or livestock inside the [footprint](chapters/terminology.qmd#term-footprint-influence). Direct crop production under or between panels is under two percent of built practice, and it carries a large share of the research attention [@stid2022; @macknick2022]. A working vocabulary has to describe the other ninety-eight percent as precisely as it describes the exception.

Where the boundary is drawn decides what counts. Most accounting stops at the fence line, the top of the modules, and a meter into the soil. This document draws it around the farm operation and the community hosting it, so a lease that keeps a farm solvent, the water leaving the field, and the habitat next door are all inside the frame.

[**Restorative agrisolar design**](chapters/terminology.qmd#term-restorative) holds that ecological, hydrological, and community function belong among a project's objectives. This document gives that claim a vocabulary that can be tested on real ground.
:::

## A shared language

A [solar grazier](chapters/terminology.qmd#term-rangevoltaics), township planner, hydrologist, and developer can describe the same eighty acres in incompatible terms. This lexicon is for the people deciding what an array does to an operation and a place.

Those decisions are being made now, and mostly in an information-poor setting: townships write ordinances without comparable data, developers and neighbors argue past each other, and several states have moved permitting authority away from the communities that host the projects [@susskind2022; @bessette2024]. Shared terms will not resolve those arguments. They let people find out what they are actually arguing about.

The build-out is not a forecast. Around 15,000 ground-mounted arrays already cover some 3,000 km² of the United States; roughly half of that ground was cropland beforehand and another third agricultural grassland [@stid2022; @sturchio2025croplands]. A net-zero grid by 2050 could put solar on 60,000–90,000 km², roughly 1% of the contiguous United States [@larson2021]. Most of what comes next will be farmland too.

## How the language works

Almost every decision in a solar project belongs to one of six groups, and this document calls them the [design levers](chapters/design-levers.qmd): scale, siting, structure, management, ownership, and contracts. They are the spine of everything else here. The [pressures](chapters/terminology.qmd#term-design-pressures) push on them, and what comes out the far end is a project's scale, its position on the [siting axis](chapters/terminology.qmd#term-siting-axis), and the [functions](chapters/terminology.qmd#term-restorative-function) the ground ends up performing.

![How the pieces fit. **Top row:** the nine design pressures converging on one site, three pushing toward restoration, three away, and three either way, which is @fig-design-pressures in miniature. They argue over the six levers, and the levers are the only things anyone can actually change. Each lever carries the colour of the [restoration mode](chapters/restoration-modes.qmd) it produces, and scale is neutral because it produces none. **Bottom row:** what a setting produces. A position on the scale transect, a position on the siting axis, the modes the setting leaves open, with one greyed to show a mode that scale has closed, and the restorative functions read as a footprint across the four outcome domains, each running from causing harm at the centre out to promoting benefit at the rim. A setting that recurs on real ground is an [archetype](chapters/archetypes.qmd), and [regionality](chapters/design-pressures.qmd#sec-regionality) changes how hard each pressure pushes, so the same levers get set differently in California and in Iowa.](figures/fig_language_structure.svg){#fig-language-structure}

Two levers carry enough internal structure to need a chapter each. **Scale** becomes the [scale transect](chapters/scale-transect.qmd), five calibration points from the farmstead to the region, because interconnection, decision-making, and ground management all move together along it. **Siting, structure, and management** jointly produce a position on the [siting axis](chapters/siting-axis.qmd), which records what happened to agricultural production: whether farming continues inside the footprint is settled by what was built and what is grown, and what the ground was beforehand is settled by where the array went.

:::  {#sec-aim-not-dimensions}
**The aim is argued; the dimensions are left to the site.** This document takes a position on what agrisolar is *for*, and refuses to fix a clearance height or a row spacing, because the same lever settings that restore ground in one region deplete it in another. [Regionality](chapters/design-pressures.qmd#sec-regionality) is where that gets explicit.
:::

## Chapter contents

| Chapter | What it holds |
|:--|:--|
| [Design Levers](chapters/design-levers.qmd) | the six decisions a project can actually make, three on the ground and two institutional, with scale setting the frame for all of them |
| [Design Pressures](chapters/design-pressures.qmd) | the nine forces arguing over how those decisions get made, where they collide, and how their weights shift by region |
| [The Scale Transect](chapters/scale-transect.qmd) | A1 to A5, farmstead to region, and how much of every other lever survives at each size |
| [The Siting Axis](chapters/siting-axis.qmd) | S1 to S5, what happened to agricultural production on the ground the array took, and which positions each scale allows |
| [Restoration Modes and Potential](chapters/restoration-modes.qmd) | which lever is made to carry the restorative work, how much each can still do at each size, why the parcel scale stands out, and the two different kinds of work called restoration |
| [Restorative Functions](chapters/restorative-functions.qmd) | the four functions a design can be aimed at, the eight outcomes they carry, and which route each benefit travels to whoever receives it |
| [Archetypal Forms](chapters/archetypes.qmd) | recurring settings of the levers that already exist on real ground, six worked through and seven sketched, from barnyard shelter to solar prairie strips |
| [Terminology](chapters/terminology.qmd) | every defined term, grouped by subject, with an [A–Z index](chapters/index-alphabetical.qmd) alongside |
| [Evidence Base and Research Needs](chapters/open-issues.qmd) | how well each claim is evidenced, stated once rather than hedged everywhere, and the measurements that would settle what is still inferred |
| [Sources](chapters/sources.qmd) | every claim traced, split into what has been verified and what still needs tracing |

## Joining in

This is a working document, and it improves by being disagreed with. Corrections,
counterexamples, and proposed terms are welcome as issues or pull requests on
[GitHub](https://github.com/MSUHydrogeology/agrisolar_lexicon). Especially useful: an archetype
that recurs in your region and is missing here, a term that lands badly with the people who have
to use it, or a citation you can trace further than we have.
